missing.usage: Extreme humorous hyperbole used when something is beyond repair or completely non-functional, combining Hawaiian 'make' (dead) with English 'die' and 'dead'.
examples: My old truck wen make die dead on H-1 dis morning, gotta call tow truck.
After surf all day at Bowls, my body wen make die dead.

missing.usage: A playful rhyming Pidgin catchphrase used to reassure someone that there is nothing to stress about.
examples: No worry, beef curry! We going make 'em on time.
You forgot your wallet? Beef curry no worry brah, I got you.

missing.usage: Used when someone suddenly breaks into loud, uncontrollable laughter at a funny joke or situation.
examples: Uncle told one joke and everybody wen bus laugh!
I had to hold back so I no bus laugh during da meeting.

missing.usage: Used when someone makes a major mistake or is caught doing something wrong and faces imminent consequences.
examples: If Mom finds out you broke her favorite bowl, your goose stay cooked!
Brah, if boss catch you sleeping, cook goose!
missing.origin: Colloquial idiom adopted in local Hawaii speech

missing.usage: To mingle effortlessly with the local crowd or hang out at a gathering without drawing unnecessary attention.
examples: Just come by da party and blend wit' da ohana.
He stay quiet at first, but now he blend real good.

missing.usage: The standard Pidgin pronunciation of 'thing', used to refer to any object, gadget, or topic.
examples: Pass me dat ting over dere on da table.
What dis ting stay called again?
